objectives: Treat fever in a child with sickle cell disease as a high-risk emergency presentation.
Recognize danger signs such as lethargy, severe pallor, and hypoxia early.
Start immediate stabilization and urgent referral rather than delayed outpatient observation.
takeaways: A 4-year-old with SCD and fever is never routine triage.
Lethargy, pallor, SpO2 93%, and tachycardia require urgent escalation.
Early referral and clear caregiver counseling reduce delays to definitive care.
learnCaseOverrides.blurb: A caregiver brings a 4-year-old with sickle cell disease, fever, and lethargy. Decide how quickly to escalate and what to do before transfer.

sections.title: Chief complaint
sections.text: Known sickle cell child with fever and reduced activity since morning

sections.title: Caregiver report
sections.text: Child is unusually sleepy, drinking poorly, and breathing faster than usual.

coach.title: Brian is high risk on arrival
coach.body: His caregiver asks if they can wait at home until tomorrow morning. Your first decision is urgency.
coach.quote: “He is very weak today and not playing at all.”

teach.label: Clinical framing
teach.text: Fever in sickle cell disease can deteriorate quickly from sepsis, severe anemia, or acute chest complications.

critical.title: High-risk SCD fever
critical.body: Lethargy + pallor + borderline hypoxia require urgent escalation.

coach.title: What is your immediate priority?
coach.body: Do not treat this as routine uncomplicated fever.

options.text: Classify as high-risk febrile SCD emergency, begin stabilization, and arrange urgent referral
Send home with oral antimalarials and return review tomorrow
Wait for child to become fully alert before deciding referral
Treat only fever with paracetamol because oxygen is above 90%

question.right: Correct. In a 4-year-old with SCD, lethargy, severe pallor, HR 148, RR 34, and SpO2 93% indicate high-risk illness requiring immediate escalation per Uganda Clinical Guidelines 2023.
question.wrong: These vitals and exam findings are not low risk. Delayed outpatient care can miss rapid decompensation in SCD children.

orders.name: Malaria RDT
orders.sub: Sample sent, referral should not wait

coach.title: How should you treat before transfer?
coach.body: Transport is being arranged and the child is still lethargic.

question.prompt: Which pre-referral plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Give oxygen support if needed, start empiric parenteral antibiotics per protocol, treat fever, and transfer urgently
Delay treatment until malaria RDT and Hb both return
Give oral AL only and reassess in OPD after 6 hours
Provide oral fluids only because BP is not recorded low

question.right: Correct. In high-risk febrile SCD children, urgent stabilization and empiric severe-infection coverage should not wait for full test completion.
question.wrong: This child has lethargy and respiratory compromise signs now. Waiting for complete labs before treatment increases risk.

rows.label: Risk context
rows.value: Known SCD, fever 38.9 C, lethargy, pallor, SpO2 93%

rows.label: Caregiver counseling
rows.value: Explained urgent need and danger signs in transit

codes.code: High-risk febrile illness in child with SCD
codes.name: Urgent pediatric referral

coach.title: Caregiver asks to wait until morning
coach.body: Choose the response that best supports urgent transfer.

options.text: Explain immediate danger based on current lethargy and breathing signs, and proceed with urgent transfer now
Agree to wait overnight since antipyretics may be enough
Avoid explanation to prevent frightening the caregiver
Cancel referral if child briefly opens eyes and drinks a sip

question.right: Correct. Counseling should reference today's danger signs so the caregiver understands why same-day transfer is lifesaving.
question.wrong: Temporary improvement does not remove high-risk status in this SCD child. Delaying referral can be dangerous.

sections.title: Case outcome
sections.text: You treated this as high-risk pediatric SCD fever and escalated early.
sections.emphasis: Early recognition and referral were the critical decisions.

coach.title: Key teaching points
coach.body: Brian's age, known sickle cell disease, lethargy, pallor, and low oxygen reserve made this an emergency presentation. Uganda Clinical Guidelines 2023 supports rapid stabilization, empiric severe-infection management, and urgent referral rather than delayed outpatient treatment.

teach.label: Clinician review
teach.text: In SCD children with fever, use a lower threshold for escalation and explain urgency clearly to caregivers.
